source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Blind expert review of 49 ideas per condition: LLM ideas rated more novel than expert human ideas, with similar feasibility. Human reranking of the AI ideas raised scores more.
numbers: 79 expert reviewers, 49 ideas per condition, 7 NLP topics. Novelty (per-idea mean, Welch t, Bonferroni): human 4.56, AI 5.18 (p=0.08), AI+human rerank 5.45 (p<0.01). Per-review test: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI+rerank 5.81 (p<0.05). Feasibility human 6.53, AI 6.30, rerank 6.41 (n.s.). Overall human 4.69, AI 4.83, rerank 5.32.
limits: NLP prompting topics only; ideas standardised in style by an LLM rewrite; reviewers judged proposals, not executed results; novelty significance depends on which of three tests is used.
agent_relevance: Novel-sounding ideas from an LLM are cheap. The open question is whether novelty judged before running predicts value. Supports G8: do not trust opinion about ideas.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (diversity)
finding: Over-generating ideas hits a wall: most new ideas repeat earlier ones.
numbers: 4000 seed ideas per topic; duplicate = cosine similarity >0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Only about 200 non-duplicate ideas out of 4000 per topic. Share of new non-duplicates falls each batch and the cumulative count plateaus.
limits: Embedding-similarity threshold is a proxy; one agent design (Claude-3.5 based).
agent_relevance: S0 problem selection by sampling many candidates gives few distinct candidates. Use code-side dedup and count distinct problems, not samples.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (LLM judges)
finding: LLM judges fail to rank ideas the way experts do; even expert reviewers agree only modestly.
numbers: Balanced top/bottom-25% agreement: human reviewers 56.1%; NeurIPS'21 66.0%; ICLR'24 71.9%; GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3, AI-Scientist reviewer 43.3; random 50.0.
limits: Ground truth is reviewer score on proposals, itself noisy.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G5/G8: the generating model should not be the selector of problems. A model scoring problem worth is near chance.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: Experts executed randomly assigned human and LLM ideas (about 103 hours each). LLM ideas lost far more score after execution than human ideas, and rankings flipped.
numbers: 43 participants completed (19 human ideas, 24 AI ideas), 58 reviewers. Score change after execution on 1-10 scale: human novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052, overall -0.628; AI novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879, overall -1.976 (p<0.05 for gap difference). Execution scores: excitement human 4.48 vs AI 3.90; effectiveness 4.78 vs 4.13 (n.s., N=43).
limits: Small N; direct comparison of execution scores not significant per idea; one LLM agent (Claude-3.5-Sonnet); NLP prompting ideas scoped to be feasible in 3 months; pre-registered hypothesis not confirmed at power.
agent_relevance: Strongest test that pre-execution ideation score mispredicts outcome. For S0: screen problems by a cheap run or check, not by a judged plan. Ideation-execution score correlation was weak (moderately negative on excitement for AI ideas).

source: Wen, Si, et al. (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Given two research ideas, predict which scores better. Off-the-shelf LLMs are near chance; a fine-tuned GPT-4.1 with paper retrieval beats NLP experts.
numbers: 1,585 test pairs (after cutoff), 6,000 training pairs. Fine-tuned system 77% on full test; GPT-4.1 untuned 51.9%; o3 about random; 25 experts 48.9% (majority), 60.0% best-per-topic ceiling; system 64.4% on the NLP expert subset; 63.6% on unpublished AI-agent ideas. Inter-annotator agreement 75.1%. GPT-3.5 fine-tuned 45.0 to 53.7%.
limits: Pairs come from published papers, so survivorship bias; relative comparison inside one topic, not choice among topics.
agent_relevance: Idea-outcome judgement is learnable from experiment records but not from prompting. A problem-selection gate could use such a reward model; our nano-loop could log its own idea-outcome pairs.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: Open-ended agent loop that generates ideas, filters them against Semantic Scholar, runs experiments and writes papers at about 15 US dollars per paper.
numbers: About 50 ideas per run per template, 12 hours on 8 H100; novelty check is a Semantic Scholar search run by the model and self-assessed per model. Automated reviewer vs human in one comparison: TPR 0.39 vs 0.52, FPR 0.31 vs 0.17. Best papers scored 5 (NeurIPS accepted average about 6).
quote: we filter ideas by connecting the language model with the Semantic Scholar API
limits: Novelty check self-assessed by the same model; reviewer is itself an LLM; small ML templates only.
agent_relevance: The one production problem-selection loop: propose, retrieve prior work, drop if too similar. The weakness is the self-judged novelty check.

source: Beel et al. (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist
finding: Independent test finds the novelty filter fails: keyword search labels known ideas as novel, and many experiments break.
numbers: 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed from coding errors; ideas such as micro-batching for SGD marked novel; median 5 citations per paper; only 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later; each code iteration adds about 8% characters.
limits: Small test (12 experiments), one system version; authors still call it a leap in automation.
agent_relevance: Retrieval-based novelty checks need real literature search, not keywords. Caps how far S0 can trust a novelty gate.

source: Gupta, Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research
finding: Experts told to look for overlap found 24% of 50 LLM research documents were paraphrased or heavily borrowed; the rest showed partial overlap and few were fully novel.
numbers: 13 experts, 50 documents (including exemplar proposals from Si et al. and AI Scientist papers); 24% plagiarised; human-written papers had a significantly lower rate (estimated from peer reviews). Automated plagiarism detectors missed the cases.
limits: Different 'presume plagiarism' framing than Si et al.; some overlap may be coincidental.
agent_relevance: Novelty judged from a shuffled review overestimates novelty. Add a code-run prior-work search before accepting a problem as new.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji, Hope (2023) SciMON
finding: Iterative novelty boosting: compare each idea to retrieved prior work and revise until it differs. GPT-4 alone gives low technical depth and low novelty.
numbers: First iteration gained novelty for about 47-56% of ideas depending on method; second iteration for 57.8%. GPT4FS+KG judged more technically detailed in 48% of pairs and less incremental in 45%. Novelty similarity threshold 0.6.
limits: Human evaluation on NLP only; GPT-4 era; novelty is versus a retrieval corpus only.
agent_relevance: A concrete operator for idea selection: retrieve neighbours, penalise similarity, revise. Code-checkable.

source: Gu, Krenn (2024-2026) Generating Interesting Scientific Ideas using Knowledge Graphs and LLMs (SciMuse)
finding: 4,451 ideas from a 58-million-paper knowledge graph rated by 110 group leaders. Ratings were modest, and graph-chosen concept pairs did not beat titles-only GPT.
numbers: Mean 2.40 on a 5-point scale (mode 1); 24.9% rated 4 or 5. High-citation-predicted pairs rated 1.94, below random pairs. Interest predicted with AUC 67.44% (GPT-4o zero-shot), 63.20% (neural net on graph features).
limits: Interest is subjective and per-person; evaluators were group leaders who took part.
agent_relevance: Network or citation-based topic hotness did not raise interest; plain LLM ranking beat graph features. Judging 'interesting' is only moderately predictable.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem
finding: Splits hypothesis discovery into retrieve inspirations, compose, rank. LLMs retrieve held-out source inspirations from a large corpus well enough to rediscover chemistry hypotheses.
numbers: Benchmark of 51 chemistry papers published after January 2024. Hit ratio of ground-truth inspirations over 75% when keeping top 20%; 71.6% when keeping 5%; 83.7% with a 4% screen (window 15 keep 3, two rounds).
limits: Ground truth is the original paper's inspirations; single domain; rediscovery is not new discovery.
agent_relevance: Shows a hypothesis can be built from background plus retrieved pieces, then ranked. Staged screening beats one-shot picking.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: Generate-debate-evolve tournament of hypotheses ranked by Elo. Elo of top hypotheses rises with more compute; Elo was checked against accuracy on GPQA.
numbers: 203 research goals; outputs split into ten time buckets; top-10 mean and best Elo rise over time with no saturation; experts rated novelty and impact on 15 curated goals against Gemini 2.0 and o1; validation cases in AML repurposing, liver fibrosis, cf-PICI.
limits: Few hypotheses validated in the lab; the evaluator is an LLM tournament; goals were chosen by humans.
agent_relevance: The research goal is given by a human; the agent picks among hypotheses, not among problems. Pairwise tournaments with search-grounded review are one selection design.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) AI Idea Bench 2025
finding: Benchmark of 3,495 AI papers and their inspiring works to score generated ideas against the real follow-up paper, avoiding knowledge leakage.
numbers: 3,495 papers; two axes: match to the original paper's content, and quality from general reference material.
limits: Only abstract and intro read this session; per-model numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: A held-out target (what was actually done next) is a code-checkable S0 test.

source: Tong et al. (2026) AI Can Learn Scientific Taste
finding: Reinforcement learning on citation-pair preferences makes a judge predict which paper gets more citations; it beats larger LLMs and transfers to later years and other fields.
numbers: 720,341 field- and time-matched pairs from 2.1M arXiv papers. In-domain 1,000 pairs: Qwen3-4B 64.7 to 80.9; Qwen3-30B 71.7 to 83.1 (position-swap consistent). Thinker win rate vs base 81.5% (30B), 76.5% (4B); average 54.2% against three strong LLM judges. Altmetric transfer: 4B 82.6%, 30B 86.3%.
limits: Citations measure attention and network, not truth; Thinker win-rates are LLM-judged; GRPO training, not a prompt scaffold.
agent_relevance: Citation-trained judgement can be learnt, but our agent has no training. Could be an external scorer of problems if available.

source: Gong, Li, Zhou (2026) LLMs learn scientific taste from institutional traces across the social sciences
finding: Fine-tuning on publication outcomes predicts the journal tier of held-out research pitches; frontier models and experts are near chance.
numbers: Four-tier task, chance 25%. Fine-tuned best accuracy 55.0% (public administration) to 85.5% (psychology). Management: Qwen3-4B 59.2% vs 48 expert gatekeepers majority 41.6%, frontier mean 31.1% (Gemini 3.1 Pro 38.8%; GPT-5.5 high about 27-31%). RL with chain-of-thought plateaued below direct fine-tuning; high-reasoning GPT-5.5 gave no gain over chat.
limits: Publication tier is a prestige signal; survivorship (only submitted work); fine-tuned weights, not scaffold.
agent_relevance: Frontier models with reasoning cannot judge which questions get published. Prompt-only problem scoring is at chance, so S0 should use cheap trials.

source: BoLeBench: Do LLMs Have Research Taste? (NeurIPS 2026 workshop)
finding: Benchmark using executed agent rollouts as ground truth. A 'pick the bolder attempt' rule beats every judge that reads full plans.
numbers: 4,059 blinded pairs, four corpora, 16 judges; best frontier judge 70.8%, nine-judge majority 67.1%; best-of-ten selection correct 36.0% vs 10% chance. No judge beats chance where the bolder attempt loses.
limits: Read from the conference listing abstract only; paper PDF not found.
agent_relevance: A cheap prior (boldness) rivals judgement. Select problems by a code-checkable feature plus execution, not a model opinion.

source: Swanson (1986) Fish oil, Raynaud's syndrome, and undiscovered public knowledge
finding: Earliest computational problem-selection method: link two literatures through shared intermediate terms to propose a hypothesis (the ABC model).
numbers: Not opened; numbers not verified.
limits: Not verified this session.
agent_relevance: Template for gap-finding by code: two concepts never co-occur but share neighbours.

source: Tshitoyan et al. (2019) Unsupervised word embeddings capture latent knowledge from materials science literature
finding: Embeddings trained on materials abstracts ranked thermoelectric candidates, and the ranking retrospectively predicted later discoveries.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not verified.
limits: Retrospective test only.
agent_relevance: Embedding-distance gap finders predict where work will go, not whether it matters.

source: Krenn, Zeilinger (2020) Predicting research trends with semantic and neural networks
finding: Semantic network of quantum physics concepts used to predict which concept pairs will be linked in future papers.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not verified.
limits: Link prediction rewards what is likely, not what is worthwhile (compare c10: high-citation-predicted pairs were not more interesting).
agent_relevance: Hot-spot prediction is possible but tends to point at crowded topics.

source: Synthesis across c03, c05, c15, c16, c17
finding: Prompted frontier LLMs judge research value near chance; trained or retrieval-augmented systems do better; execution results disagree with idea ratings.
numbers: Prompted pairwise accuracy: 45-53% (Si), 51.9% GPT-4.1 (Wen), 31.1% on a 4-class task with 25% chance (Gong), 36% best-of-ten vs 10% (BoLeBench). Trained: 77% (Wen), 59.2% (Gong), 80.9-83.1% on citation pairs (Tong).
limits: Tasks differ (idea quality, tier, citations), so numbers are not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Design rule: no model-opinion gate for S0; use retrieval check, cheap execution, and a trained scorer where available.

source: Wen et al. (2025) robustness checks
finding: Showed the 77% was not from superficial cues; abstracts alone bias toward older ideas.
numbers: Annotator mislabel rate fell from 11% to 2.5% over review rounds; one input-form ablation moved accuracy from 38.8% to 53.0%; unsupported-claims subset 68.5% vs 81.1% cleared.
limits: Details of each ablation not all recorded.
agent_relevance: Beware leakage: age and complexity cues give fake signal. Same for any internal problem-scoring.

source: Si et al. (2025) execution study, unit of analysis
finding: With each review as a data point (N=181), human ideas beat AI ideas on excitement, effectiveness, soundness and overall, but not novelty; per idea (N=43) nothing is significant.
numbers: N=181 reviews: one-sided t-tests significant on 4 of 5 metrics; N=43 ideas: FDR p-values 0.586, 0.175, 0.266, 0.175.
limits: Result depends on the unit of analysis (pseudo-replication risk).
agent_relevance: Do not over-read either direction; the within-idea gap is the robust result.

source: Lu et al. (2024) AI Scientist failure modes
finding: Authors note the novelty check is self-assessed by each model so cross-model novelty is unreliable, and list failures: hallucinated results and file paths.
numbers: Runs of about 50 ideas; parallelising idea generation did not change mean review score.
limits: Self-reported; independent test (Beel) found more failures.
agent_relevance: Confirms G8: separate generator from verifier for novelty.

source: Gupta, Pruthi (2025) distinguishability
finding: LLM proposals separated from human ones in embedding space, and detection tools did not catch plagiarised ones.
numbers: PCA of embeddings separates the groups; automated plagiarism detectors failed on matched documents.
limits: Visual embedding result only.
agent_relevance: Embedding distance to prior work is a cheap code check for derivative problems.

source: Si et al. (2024) homogenisation warning
finding: Authors warn AI ideation could narrow idea diversity across the field.
numbers: Based on the 200-of-4000 non-duplicate result.
limits: Discussion section, opinion.
agent_relevance: If many agents pick problems with the same model, picks converge. Add a diversity count to the S0 gate.

source: Tong et al. (2026) temporal and controlled tests
finding: Judge keeps gains on 2025 papers never seen and on same-author and topic-matched pairs.
numbers: 904 temporal-OOD pairs; 541 same-faculty pairs; 245 embedding-matched topic-control pairs; 160 bioRxiv pairs.
limits: Per-model figures for these sets not copied; citations are a noisy impact proxy.
agent_relevance: Impact signal survives author and topic controls, so it is not only reputation.

source: Gong et al. (2026) calibration and failure modes
finding: Fine-tuned judge confidence is calibrated, so triage on high-confidence picks gets high accuracy; frontier models collapse into one tier.
numbers: Frontier collapse: 87% of articles put in one tier, macro F1 0.145; expert individual mean 36.2%, majority 41.6% on 89 of 120 articles with a clear plurality.
limits: Per-field triage accuracy not recorded.
agent_relevance: Abstention-by-confidence is a pattern for a problem scorer, but G6 forbids abstaining on the first pass.
